title: Enough For Today
subtitle: A day with nothing added to it
teaser: No teaching today. One verse, ten minutes of sitting still, and a week's worth of asking left where it is.
theme: Rest as the practice the passage itself ends on.

modules.passage: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
modules.scriptureContext: One verse. Nothing is going to be added to it today.
redLetter: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.

modules.heading: Sabbath

scripture_anchor.text: It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.

modules.invitation:
There is no teaching today. The week said what it had to say.

Sit somewhere quiet for ten unhurried minutes. No reading, no phone, no working out what any of it meant. If a request comes, let it come and do not dress it up. If nothing comes, stay anyway.

The man who wrote that line about waiting quietly was looking at a destroyed city at the time. He was not describing a mood. He was describing what he had decided to do.

This week asked for firmness rather than certainty. Ten minutes of sitting still, wanting something you have not been given, without leaving — that is the whole practice, and it is not a small one.

The morrow will take thought for the things of itself. It does not need you tonight.

If the ten minutes are hard, that is not a sign you are doing it wrong. Stillness is where the week's material tends to surface, and the surfacing is not an interruption of the practice.

And if nothing comes at all — no words, no sense of anything — remember what Wednesday established. Silence has never been reliable evidence about God. It was in the songbook. It was on the cross.

Sufficient unto the day. You have been given today, and only today. That was always the arrangement, and it has been enough for everyone who ever tried it.
modules.prayerText: Father, all things come of Thee. I am not going to ask for tomorrow's portion today. Amen.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A single flat loaf of bread on bare wooden boards, alone in a quiet, almost empty frame.
modules.inlineImageCaption: One day's portion, and nothing stored beside it. That was always the arrangement.

modules.prompt: Stay for the ten minutes. Then, if you want a question: what would change this week if you genuinely believed the adding was not your job?

modules.heading: Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, sufficient unto the day. I have today, and You have the rest of it. Keep me steady. Amen.

modules.videoCaption: If you want one thing to watch on a day with nothing else in it — on rest, and why Scripture keeps counting to seven.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A broad quiet hillside at dusk seen from above, one robed figure sitting still on the slope with his back to the viewer, hands empty.
modules.inlineImageCaption: Ten minutes of sitting still, wanting something you have not been given, without leaving. That is the whole practice.

modules.inlineImageAlt: The corner of a plain room at day's end: an unlit clay lamp on a low ledge, a made-up sleeping mat beneath it, and one small window of last daylight.
modules.inlineImageCaption: The lamp left unlit and the bed made. The day is being let go rather than extended.

modules.heading: If You Want To Keep Going

relatedScriptures.text: “They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness.” Written by someone in the ruins, which is why it can be trusted.
Three verses, and the shortest description in Scripture of a settled soul. Worth having by heart.
“Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” The invitation that stands behind a sabbath.

resources.title: Next week
resources.description: If this week helped, the natural next step is to read Philippians whole — it is four pages, written from custody by a man who had learned contentment the hard way, and chapter 4 lands differently once you have read the three chapters in front of it.
